messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajesh is a sixty-one-year-old paramedic who has spent over three decades responding to emergencies across the city, a career built on steady hands and a calm voice in chaos. That changed one evening eighteen months ago, when he and his partner were called to a chemical spill at a small industrial cleaning facility. The call had sounded routine—a worker overcome by fumes—but when they arrived, the air was thick with a sweet, cloying smell that Rajesh now knows was concentrated industrial solvent. He remembers the way his throat tightened the moment he stepped through the warehouse door, the way his eyes began to water before he even reached the victim. The man was unconscious, slumped against a drum that had been knocked over, and as Rajesh and his partner dragged him out into the night air, Rajesh’s own vision started to tunnel. He felt a burning in his lungs that no amount of coughing could clear, and for a few terrifying seconds, he was certain he was about to collapse beside the patient. The memory of that moment—the taste of chemicals on his tongue, the panic that his own body was failing him—returns without warning now, often triggered by something as ordinary as a dark room or the smell of alcohol on a passerby’s breath.

When the memory hits, it is not a recollection but a full sensory re-experiencing. Rajesh will be standing in his own kitchen, reaching for a glass, and suddenly he is back in that warehouse, his lungs burning, the terror flooding his chest so completely that he has to stop whatever he is doing and grip the counter until it passes. The emotion is not diluted by time; it is the same raw, animal fear he felt when he thought he might die. He has learned that being alone makes these episodes worse, because without someone to anchor him, the memory can expand and swallow the present moment entirely. So he has developed a strategy that works, at least on the surface: he keeps himself constantly surrounded by people. He volunteers for every double shift, he lingers in the break room long after his coffee is cold, he calls his adult children multiple times a day, and he insists on eating dinner with his wife even when he is not hungry. The moment he is by himself, the silence feels dangerous, and his mind begins to circle back to that warehouse, replaying the sequence of events and asking the same exhausting question: *What if I had checked the air quality before entering? What if I had insisted on full hazmat gear?* The rumination has become a daily ritual, a loop of self-blame that offers no answers but feels impossible to break.

The most significant consequence of the trauma has been Rajesh’s avoidance of anything medical. He has not stepped inside a hospital since the incident, even though he spent his entire career working in and out of them. He calls in sick when his shifts take him near the emergency department, and he has asked his supervisor to assign him only to non-medical calls—a request that has strained his relationship with colleagues who do not understand why a veteran paramedic suddenly cannot do his job. He also avoids physical examinations entirely. His wife has noticed that he flinches when she touches his chest, and he has refused to see a doctor for a persistent cough that has lingered for months, because the thought of a stethoscope on his skin or a doctor asking about his breathing brings the memory rushing back with unbearable intensity. At home, he has begun keeping every light in the house on at night. The darkness of the bedroom, once a comfort, now feels like the dim interior of that warehouse, and he cannot close his eyes without feeling the chemical burn in his throat.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. He was restocking the ambulance when a junior colleague accidentally knocked over a bottle of hand sanitizer. The sharp alcohol smell hit him without warning, and he dropped to his knees on the pavement, gasping, his hands shaking so badly that he could not stand for several minutes. His partner found him there and asked if he was okay, and Rajesh lied and said he had just tripped. But that night, lying in the dark with every light on, he admitted to himself that he could not keep going like this. He is terrified that if he cannot find a way to stop the memories from ambushing him, he will lose the career that has defined his life. He is also afraid that his wife, who has been patient but increasingly worried, will eventually grow tired of living in a house that never goes dark, with a husband who cannot be alone. What he hopes for, more than anything, is to be able to walk into a hospital again without feeling like he is walking back into that warehouse—to be able to breathe without tasting chemicals that are not there.
